sections.html:
Idaho's second largest city after Boise, Meridian lies in Ada County. A July 1, 2025 estimate puts residents at 142,988, compared with 117,635 in the 2020 count, and no other Idaho city has grown faster.

About 26.8 square miles of flat ground in the north central Treasure Valley belong to Meridian, with Boise on one side and Nampa on the other. Scale and new construction mean your house competes against a deep supply of listings. Owners with repair needs or a tight timeline often weigh other routes for that reason.

Farming and canals built this place. The Nampa-Meridian and Settlers irrigation districts continue to serve it, and canals cut across town from southeast to northwest. Old irrigation easements and lot lines still reflect that.

Before selling, learn whether your parcel gets pressurized irrigation or carries a ditch right. Buyers raise the question, and a ready answer saves time. Your title company can help trace it if the closing papers are silent.

Nearly all of Meridian sits north of I-84. Street names begin with a compass prefix measured from Franklin Road and Meridian Road. West to east, the big roads are Black Cat, Ten Mile, Linder, Meridian, Locust Grove and Eagle. North to south: Chinden (Highway 20/26), McMillan, Ustick, Cherry or Fairview, Franklin, Overland, Victory and Amity.

Old Town is built around Main Street and Pine Street. Industrial land follows the railroad between Pine and Franklin. People shop by the closest major intersection, so mention yours when you describe the property to any buyer.

Summers here are hot and dry, winters cold with a little light snow. Readings above 100 F are common, which puts cooling ahead of winter loads. Inspectors look hardest at the air conditioner's age, attic insulation and ventilation, windows and sprinklers.

A dead cooling unit is expensive to swap out right before closing. Cash buyers generally subtract that cost from their offer rather than insisting you handle it.

Permits for structural, fire, electrical, mechanical and plumbing work go through Meridian Building Services, 33 E. Broadway Ave. #102. Hours are Monday to Friday, 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM, and the line is 208-887-2211.

Applications, fees and inspection bookings are handled in the city's online citizen portal. Once every inspection is signed off, the city issues a certificate of occupancy. Remodels, fences, sheds, garages, foundations, fireplaces and demolition are all permitted work.

  • Search the permit history for garages, sheds and remodels before you list.
  • Finish any open permit you can. An unclosed one may hold up a closing.
  • Store the final inspection sign-offs with your other house records.

Planning and Zoning decisions shape what gets built nearby. If your lot adjoins vacant land, read the City Council hearing agendas. Council meets on Tuesdays: work session at 4:30 p.m., public hearings at 6:00 p.m.

West Ada, the biggest district in Idaho, covers nearly all of Meridian. One part of town falls under Kuna Joint School District 3. Ask the district itself which school serves your address rather than inferring it from the city name, or look at the district named on your tax bill.

Ada County sends Meridian's tax bills. Pay everything, or the first half, by December 20. The remaining half is due June 20, provided the first half arrived on time.

DateWhat happens in Ada County
January 1Appraisers set market value; first day to apply for the homeowner's exemption
First Monday in JuneAssessment notices mailed
June 20Second half due
Fourth Monday in JuneLast day to appeal a value
Fourth Monday in NovemberPrimary roll bills mailed (by this date)
December 20Full-year payment or first half due

A weekend or holiday on the 20th pushes the deadline to the next business day for anything postmarked by the 20th. The county also mails subsequent and missed roll bills for improvements and later-assessed property, payable June 20. A recently built or remodeled house is the likely candidate, so have your title company search for them.

An owner-occupied primary residence gets an exemption worth 50% of its value, covering up to one acre and capped at $125,000. It ends when the property changes hands, so the next owner files a new application.

Idaho puts no limit on how far assessed value can move. A taxing district may grow the property tax part of its budget by 3% at most, unless voters approve more or new construction and annexation widen the base. Questions go to taxinfo@adacounty.id.gov or 208-287-6800.

Under Idaho Code 55-2504, whoever transfers a residence of one to four units fills out a property condition disclosure form. Rentals that the owner does not occupy are included, and so are exchanges, installment contracts and options as well as sales.

Idaho Code 55-2505 lists exceptions: foreclosure transfers, a fiduciary's estate transfers, transfers to a spouse or lineal relative, and brand new homes nobody has lived in. That last group still declares annexation and city service status. An Idaho attorney or title officer can tell you where you stand.

Owing tax does not stop a sale. The title company reads the county records before closing, finds what is unpaid and subtracts it from your proceeds at the closing table. That is also true for any mortgage balance.

The cleaner your records, the quicker this goes. Pull the latest bill from Ada County, check whether a subsequent or missed roll bill exists, and tell the buyer about anything still open. Surprises found late in the process are what stretch a closing out, and a cash buyer who hears about them on day one can price them in.

If you are behind on payments and the clock matters, say so when you ask for an offer. A buyer who knows your deadline can often pick a closing date to match it.

No lender means no loan approval delay. Your schedule comes down to title work and the closing date you pick.

  1. Request an offer and describe occupancy, liens, back taxes and repairs you know about.
  2. The buyer walks through the house.
  3. Set the offer beside listing costs, repair quotes and the cost of carrying the house.
  4. If you say yes, a title company handles closing and clears any mortgage or tax debt out of your proceeds.

Declining costs nothing. Meridian's market is big, and a house in good shape may do well on the open market, so a local agent's view is a fair benchmark.

Gather your latest tax bill, permit paperwork and a list of known repairs first. With those in hand the offer is tighter and the closing moves faster.

faqs.q: Who sends property tax bills in Meridian?
faqs.a: Ada County. Pay the whole amount or the first half by December 20, and the rest by June 20 if the first half was on time.

faqs.q: When must I appeal a Meridian assessment?
faqs.a: By the fourth Monday in June. The Ada County Assessor mails notices on the first Monday of that month.

faqs.q: How do I find permit records for my Meridian house?
faqs.a: Call Meridian Building Services at 208-887-2211 or visit 33 E. Broadway Ave. #102. The online citizen portal also tracks permits and inspections.
West Ada covers most of the city and is Idaho's largest. A portion lies in Kuna Joint School District 3.

faqs.q: Will the buyer keep my homeowner's exemption?
faqs.a: No. It ends at the sale, and the new owner applies through the county assessor if the house will be their primary residence.
